description: Apex G, a dedicated two-person research team competing in NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our focus is on rigorous scientific research, comparative planetary geology, and building a high-impact research paper evaluating terrestrial analogs for lunar and Martian exploration. We bring strong skills in data analysis, scientific writing, and geospatial evaluation. We are looking for a collaborative spirit who shares our ambition to produce top-tier academic-style research under a hackathon timeline.
summary: We developed a multi-dimensional trade study and quantitative evaluation framework to assess the Pingualuit Impact Crater in Nunavik, Québec, as a terrestrial analog for Shackleton Crater at the lunar South Pole. Using NASA LROC, LOLA, ShadowCam, and Earth observation datasets, our team evaluated both sites across eight key dimensions: geology, topography, temperature and illumination, water and permafrost, surface erosion, biology, subsurface structures, and mission operations. By scoring each dimension and conducting a rigorous physical gap analysis, we identified where Pingualuit effectively simulates lunar polar conditions, such as impact morphology and continuous permafrost preservation, while explicitly accounting for terrestrial limitations like gravity, atmosphere, and biological activity. This work is critical for future Artemis and robotic missions, providing mission planners with a scientifically defensible, dimension-specific analog baseline to test surface operations, subsurface sensing, and planetary protection protocols on Earth before deploying hardware to the Moon.
details:
Project Overview and Functionality

Our team developed a quantitative trade study to evaluate the Pingualuit Impact Crater in Nunavik, Quebec, as a terrestrial analog for Shackleton Crater at the lunar South Pole. We built an eight-dimension Analog Similarity Index scoring model to systematically compare the geological, topographical, and environmental features of both locations.

Tools, Datasets, and Software

We utilized orbital and spatial datasets including NASA LROC QuickMap, LOLA, ShadowCam, ASTER Digital Elevation Models, and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to conduct our topographical and morphological analysis.

Benefits and Intended Impact

This research gives Artemis mission planners and lunar base designers a structured, science-based analog baseline. It allows engineering teams to test robotic rovers, subsurface radar sensors, permafrost sampling methods, and surface operations in a harsh earthly environment before deploying hardware to the Moon.

Creativity and Key Factors Considered

Instead of assuming a simple one-to-one match, our framework uses a zero to ten scoring system across eight distinct evaluation categories. We focused heavily on scientific honesty by explicitly scoring and accounting for major terrestrial differences, such as Earth atmosphere, standard gravity, and an active lake biosphere, versus the lunar vacuum, low gravity, and permanently shadowed regions.
